q: Fill up: In pregnancy, tidal volume increases by about ______%, which lowers maternal arterial PCO2 to roughly ______ mmHg.
exp: Progesterone-driven hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 to about 30-32 mmHg, creating the gradient for fetal carbon dioxide transfer.

sec: Maternal oxygen dynamics, endocrine & visceral changes
q: Which of the following statements about respiratory physiology in pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: The fall in maternal PaCO2 is what allows fetal carbon dioxide to diffuse into maternal blood
Maternal arterial PO2 falls markedly because oxygen consumption outstrips the rise in ventilation
The gravid uterus pushes the diaphragm downwards, increasing the antero-posterior chest diameter
Functional residual capacity rises during pregnancy, giving the mother more oxygen reserve
exp: PaO2 is normal or slightly higher, the diaphragm rises (transverse diameter widens) and FRC falls, so the pregnant woman desaturates faster.

sec: Iron requirements, metabolism & Anemia Mukt Bharat / I-NIPI
q: Fill up: The total extra iron requirement of a pregnancy is about ______ mg, of which roughly ______ mg goes to the fetus and placenta.
exp: About 1000 mg extra iron is needed in total: the largest share expands the maternal red cell mass and about 300 mg goes to the fetus and placenta.

q: Fill up: Anaemia in pregnancy is diagnosed when the haemoglobin is below ______ g/dL, and severe anaemia when it is below ______ g/dL.
exp: WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as haemoglobin below 11 g/dL, with severe anaemia below 7 g/dL and moderate between 7 and 9.9 g/dL.

sec: Maternal & fetal complications of anemia in pregnancy
q: All of the following are recognised consequences of severe maternal anaemia EXCEPT:
opts: Fetal macrosomia
Preterm labour and low birth weight
High-output cardiac failure
Postpartum haemorrhage from poor myometrial contractility
exp: Severe anaemia impairs oxygen transfer and myometrial function, so growth restriction and preterm birth occur; macrosomia does not.

sec: Clinical evaluation & physical workup of gestational anemia
q: A 26-year-old at 30 weeks has a haemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL with pallor, koilonychia, a smooth sore tongue and pica. Which single investigation best confirms the underlying diagnosis?
opts: Serum ferritin estimation
Serum vitamin B12 assay
Haemoglobin electrophoresis
Direct Coombs test
exp: Koilonychia, glossitis and pica point to iron deficiency, and serum ferritin is the most specific single test of iron stores.

sec: Diagnostic RBC indices & iron profile interpretation
q: Match the laboratory pattern with the diagnosis — 1) Microcytic hypochromic cells with a low ferritin 2) Macrocytic cells with hypersegmented neutrophils 3) Microcytosis with a normal ferritin and a raised HbA2 … A) Beta thalassaemia trait B) Iron deficiency anaemia C) Folate or vitamin B12 deficiency
exp: Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils means megaloblastosis, and a raised HbA2 with normal iron means thalassaemia trait.

sec: Oral iron therapy & assessing treatment response
q: Fill up: An adequate response to oral iron is a haemoglobin rise of about ______ g/dL over ______ weeks.
exp: A rise of roughly 1 g/dL in 3-4 weeks confirms adherence and absorption; failure prompts a search for malabsorption or non-iron causes.

sec: Parenteral iron therapy, Ganzoni formula & blood transfusion
q: Which of the following statements about parenteral iron in pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Iron sucrose is the preferred parenteral preparation; iron dextran needs a test dose because of anaphylaxis risk
Intramuscular iron into the gluteal region is the preferred parenteral route in the third trimester
Total-dose iron infusion is the treatment of choice in the first trimester for severe anaemia
Parenteral iron must never be given once the haemoglobin has fallen below 7 g/dL
exp: Iron sucrose and ferric carboxymaltose are safe after the first trimester; iron dextran risks anaphylaxis, and intramuscular iron is painful and stains the skin.

sec: Trimester-wise gestational management protocol for anemia
q: A primigravida at 14 weeks has a haemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL with breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs. What is the most appropriate plan?
opts: Admit, start parenteral iron sucrose, continue oral iron to term and recheck the haemoglobin in four weeks
Transfuse packed cells immediately and deliver the pregnancy whatever the gestation
Continue oral iron alone and review the haemoglobin at 28 weeks
Recommend termination because severe anaemia before viability is unmanageable
exp: In the second trimester a symptomatic woman with severe anaemia needs parenteral iron; transfusion is reserved for decompensation or an imminent need for delivery.

sec: Antimicrobial safety & teratogenic hazards in pregnancy
q: All of the following antimicrobials are regarded as safe in pregnancy EXCEPT:
opts: Tetracyclines
Penicillins
Cephalosporins
Macrolides such as erythromycin
exp: Tetracyclines stain fetal teeth and bones and are avoided; penicillins, cephalosporins and macrolides are safe in pregnancy.

q: Match the exposure with its fetal consequence — 1) Warfarin between 6 and 12 weeks 2) Warfarin near term and in labour 3) Low molecular weight heparin … A) Does not cross the placenta and is the preferred agent B) Warfarin embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses C) Fetal and neonatal intracranial haemorrhage during delivery
exp: Warfarin teratogenicity peaks in organogenesis, near-term use risks fetal bleeding, and heparin molecules do not cross the placenta.

q: Fill up: The critical window for warfarin embryopathy is between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
exp: Exposure from 6 to 12 weeks produces nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata; later exposure mainly risks central nervous system and bleeding problems.

sec: Maternal cardiovascular hemodynamics & peak stress periods
q: Fill up: Maternal cardiac output rises by about ______% in pregnancy and peaks around ______ weeks.
exp: Output rises early and peaks at 20-24 weeks; further surges occur during labour and immediately after delivery.

sec: Heart failure vs pregnancy signs, RHD & congenital lesions
q: Which of the following best distinguishes pathological heart disease from the normal cardiovascular changes of pregnancy?
opts: A loud P2, a third heart sound and persistent basal crepitations are pathological, while a soft systolic flow murmur is not
Exertional dyspnoea in a pregnant woman is always pathological and needs echocardiography
Any systolic murmur heard over the pulmonary area in pregnancy indicates organic valve disease
Pedal oedema in the third trimester always indicates incipient cardiac failure
exp: Breathlessness, a soft ejection murmur and ankle oedema are common in normal pregnancy; a loud P2, gallop rhythm and persistent crepitations are not.

sec: Lesion prognosis & WHO class IV contraindications
q: All of the following are WHO class IV lesions in which pregnancy is contraindicated EXCEPT:
opts: Mild mitral stenosis in NYHA class I
Pulmonary arterial hypertension of any cause
Severe left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction below 30%
Severe mitral stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension
exp: Mild mitral stenosis with good functional class is a class II lesion with a small risk; the others carry prohibitive maternal mortality.

sec: Intrapartum & postpartum management of heart disease
q: A primigravida with tight mitral stenosis reaches full cervical dilatation. Which intrapartum measure matters most for her safety?
opts: Cut the second stage short with forceps or vacuum under epidural analgesia and avoid Valsalva pushing
Encourage a long second stage of spontaneous pushing to avoid any instrumentation
Give intramuscular ergometrine with the delivery of the anterior shoulder
Withhold analgesia so that warning symptoms of failure are not masked
exp: Epidural analgesia and instrumental shortening of the second stage blunt the dangerous cardiac output surges, and ergometrine is avoided.

q: Match the lesion with its description — 1) Peripartum cardiomyopathy 2) Mitral stenosis 3) Severe aortic stenosis … A) Systolic dysfunction appearing in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after delivery B) Diastolic murmur with a loud first sound and opening snap; tachycardia is poorly tolerated C) Fixed cardiac output, so obstruction makes labour and delivery extremely dangerous
exp: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is defined by its timing, mitral stenosis is a diastolic lesion that cannot raise output through tachycardia, and aortic stenosis fixes output.
